analysis.one_liner: Lets consumers lock their credit files for free so identity thieves cannot open accounts in their name.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: after being referred to the Senate Banking Committee in July 2005, it sat there until the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let any consumer demand a "security freeze" on their credit file. Once frozen, the credit reporting companies could not release the file to anyone opening new credit, insurance, or employment screening without the consumer unlocking it with a personal code, and they could not charge any fee for freezing, unlocking, or temporarily lifting it. It gave the Federal Trade Commission enforcement power and let consumers sue agencies that violated the rules. The bill never left the Senate Banking Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who want to stop identity thieves from opening accounts in their name, and anyone tired of their credit data being sold for marketing and prescreened offers.

how_it_helps.text: Any consumer could place a security freeze on their file by certified mail, phone, or secure email, and the agency must do it within 2 business days (or 24 hours by secure email) [S3].
The freeze blocks the agency from releasing the file for new credit, insurance, or employment decisions, and a third party denied access may only treat the application as incomplete [S3].
Consumers can temporarily lift the freeze for a specific lender within 3 business days, so legitimate borrowing still works [S3].
Credit reporting agencies may not charge any fee for placing, lifting, or temporarily opening a freeze, and only a $5 fee for repeated replacement of a lost password [S3].
A freeze request made to one agency must be honored by every other consumer reporting agency in the country that keeps a file on that consumer [S3].
The FTC gets rulemaking and enforcement powers, consumers can complain to the FTC or their state attorney general, and consumers can sue agencies that violate the freeze rules [S2] [S3].

The bill defines the protected file to include information used for commercial marketing, political campaigns, and charitable solicitation, and it restricts sharing of medical payment data even among corporate affiliates [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit reporting agencies lose fee income they collected in many states for freeze services and lose the ability to sell frozen consumers' data for prescreened offers, marketing lists, and insurance or employment screening. Lenders and data brokers face a small friction cost when a consumer forgets to lift a freeze.

drawbacks.text: A freeze adds friction to ordinary life: a consumer who forgets to lift it can face delays of up to 3 business days on a legitimate loan, car purchase, or apartment application, and a third party can treat the application as incomplete [S3].
The freeze is only as strong as the consumer's guard on their own PIN or password, and the bill allows a $5 charge for each repeated reissue of a lost code [S3].

The definition of the protected file excludes a consumer's transactions with a company itself and most sharing among corporate affiliates, so the freeze blocks third-party access more than intra-company data flows [S3].
Mandatory access carve-outs for law enforcement, child support, tax, and health-fraud agencies, and for existing creditors reviewing accounts, narrow what the freeze can stop [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is strong and targeted: identity theft through new-account fraud is exactly what a credit freeze prevents, and the bill removes the fee barriers that made freezes rare in 2005. The costs are real but modest — application delays when a consumer forgets to lift the freeze, and lost convenience for data-driven marketing. An honest weakness is that the bill relied on consumers acting for themselves; it offered no default protection. Weighing that, the benefits to ordinary people substantially outweigh the friction costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Shelby introduced the bill on July 21, 2005 [S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day [S5].
No committee action, floor vote, or companion House action followed, and the bill had zero cosponsors [S4] [S5].
The 109th Congress ended January 3, 2007, and the bill died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The credit reporting industry is better off: it kept charging consumers for freeze services in states that allowed them and kept unrestricted access to sell consumer files for prescreened offers, marketing lists, and data products. A national free freeze would have cut that revenue and blocked that data sales channel.

for.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
for.role: U.S. Senator from Alabama and Chairman, Senate Banking Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks, but never brought it up in the committee he chaired

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the remaining year and a half of the Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote

against.name: Consumer reporting and data broker industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory free security freezes, which would have eliminated freeze fees and cut off access to consumer files for prescreened credit offers and marketing

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no partisan split is on the record; the only Senate action was a single Republican sponsor introducing the bill with zero cosponsors of either party [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Bureaus were charging consumers fees to place and lift freezes under state laws; this bill bans those fees nationwide and forces the freeze to propagate to every bureau's file. It also blocks them from selling frozen consumers' data for prescreened offers and marketing.

industries.industry: Data brokers and marketing list providers
industries.note: The protected file explicitly covers data used for commercial marketing, political campaigns, and charitable solicitation, so a freeze shuts them out of selling that data.

industries.industry: Lenders, insurers, and employers using background screening
industries.note: They lose instant access to applicants' files and can treat frozen applications as incomplete, but consumers can lift a freeze within 3 business days for a specific lender, and existing creditors retain account-review access.
